response.title: A Garden's Water Record
response.passage: At West Gate High, the science club began collecting notes about a neighborhood garden after a month with little rain. Their first task was to observe when each plot needed water, rather than guess from the dry soil on the surface. The gardeners cooperated by sharing a notebook, although they disagreed about whether young plants should be watered every day. A reliable pattern appeared only after the students compared notes from several warm and cool days. The group found that the shallow reservoir behind the school was lower than usual, which meant a shortage could become serious if the dry spell continued. Instead of asking everyone to stop watering, the club suggested that each family reserve a bucket of rainwater when possible and water plants early. Some residents welcomed the plan; others worried that it asked too much of families with little time. The students listened to that concern and changed the chart so that recording water use took less than a minute. By the end of the month, more families were using the chart, but the reservoir level had not yet recovered. The club therefore described its result carefully: the project improved how people shared water, but it had not proved that neighborhood use was lower. For the next dry season, the students plan to compare the same months across two years before making a larger claim.

items.answer: A school club used shared records to help neighbors manage garden water carefully.

items.answer: Keeping the record might take too much time.

response.title: Two Visits to the River
response.passage: Each spring, students at Brookside High record the current water level in a small river behind the gym. Before measuring, the students marked two safe places along the bank. During one morning walk, Ana noticed that a fallen branch divided the flow into two paths. Leaves on the wider side traveled faster, while those near the bank barely moved. Her teacher explained that a river current can change from one place to another, even on the same day. The class returned after lunch and found that recent rain had raised the water level. Because the branch was still there, the students could compare how the same obstacle affected stronger water. Their notes showed that the main current had pushed leaves past the second marker in less time. The class added both visits to its chart instead of treating the first result as a permanent pattern. The teacher said repeated observations helped them describe conditions without claiming that every river behaves the same way.

items.question: What does current mean in the first sentence?
items.answer: Happening now or at this time.
distractors: Moving steadily in one direction.
Likely to happen in the future.
Having no connection to the present.

items.question: What did Ana notice about the leaves?
items.answer: They traveled faster on the wider side of the branch.
distractors: They all stopped beside the bank.

They passed the second marker before the class arrived.

items.question: Why did the class return after lunch?
items.answer: To compare observations after the rain changed the water level.

items.answer: Repeated observations give a fuller account of changing conditions.
distractors: One morning observation can describe every river.
A chart should include only the fastest-moving leaves.
A river's flow cannot change around an obstacle.
